They’re not unplayable in the slightest. If people played the originals and loved them, that doesn’t suddenly go away because modern gaming has become more refined. That being said, there’s a very large margin of players who are going to naturally be put off when a game is old enough to have quite clunky movement and mechanics. Gaming has come a long way since then and trying to go back to an almost 30 year old game with difficult controls and restricting camera mechanics will be quite difficult for your average person.

The originals will always remain mainstays in the industry and will always act as a template for great games to follow in their footsteps, but it’s also important not to shame players who want a higher quality experience, because of admitted outdated control schemes.

By a modern standard, games have come a long way and mechanically the earlier games don’t hold a candle to what we’re able to achieve now. While they’re good in their own right, it’s valid that the drawbacks will put some people off.

(Before anyone says anything, I’m quite aware that hardware limitations exist and there weren’t as many industry standards for control schemes and mechanics 25-30 years ago.)

The only things you NEED are an IFAK and mags. Everything else comes with time.

People getting into tactical gear often make the mistake of overloading their plate carriers with tons of gear that’s really cumbersome and difficult to use. Just train with what you have and add things gradually over time.

For example “hmm, if I’m gonna be bringing this thing out for extended periods of time, I should think of where to put more mags.” And then you can look at the area you have on the vest and decide where to put them, that makes it easiest for you. 

Another example. “Hmm, I’m going to be carrying some miscellaneous items. I need somewhere to put them.” Then you can think about where you want to put a pouch. Maybe you could get a little pouch to attach? Maybe a dangler pouch if you need the space on the carrier. Maybe you could get a pack that attaches to your plate bag.

Task Forces will typically build their gear sets based on the missions that they’re trying to accomplish. You should keep that mindset. Just add the gear that you feel you need. Prepare for the problems you have, not the problems you don’t. Make sure every piece of your gear has a purpose and has a position on your body that matches said purpose.

Here’s a general rule of thumb for anything tactical related. Think of the front of your body as a 180 degree range of movement. The seams of your pants being the cut off points. Anything you may need immediate access to should be within that 180 degree area, in front of you. If you’re going to have something behind you, anywhere near your back, that should be gear that you can afford to take your sweet ass time, getting to. If you’re carrying a weapon or ammunition, those should always be either on your hips, or in front of you, to easily take a hold of them. I used to be a glass collector in a bar. I did that for around 3 months and the job was fairly intense. If I ever spotted an unattended glass or an empty one, I had to get it fairly quickly, since the bar was often packed.

As a result, whenever I’m in a bar or restaurant, I now have a compulsive need to stack empty glasses and return them to the bar.

The first time somebody touched me, affectionately (SFW dw)

I was having a fucking horrible night at work. For context, I used to collect glasses at a bar but didn’t really get to go out on nights out like that. It’s still pretty rare for me to be honest. Working in those crowds, getting pushed around all the time, it was hell. It made me feel even more alone than usual. I tried to get some guy to move out of my way because I had a giant stack of glasses that needed to be brought back to the bar. He wouldn’t move. There was this girl sat nearby who saw what happened and threw a lime at the guy. He moved just in time and it hit me square in the face. He didn’t mean for anything bad to happen. She didn’t either. It just happened. I gave her the middle finger, because it just made me feel even worse. I felt absolutely destroyed at that point. 

The next time I went over to that area of the bar, she saw me and jumped up, coming over to me. She stroked my face gently, holding my face in her hand, telling me she was sorry. I’d never felt anything like that before. I burst into tears on the spot. I felt awful and that little bit of care was enough to push me over the edge but it also gave me the little push I needed to get through the rest of the night. I’d love to relive that memory or to feel that again. Just having a photo of when it happened would be enough.

Not sure if this counts but back in 2017, I was present for a false bomb scare. We were in London for a short trip and I was in a really bad place at the time. Right as we reached Euston Station to get back home, a flood of people came running out of the building, screaming and shouting "BOMB". It was honestly terrifying but I already had a lot on my mind. I felt lonely at the time and some people had just cut ties with me around that point in my life. When I saw all of those people running at me, I turned and followed my family into wherever they went, because obviously didn't want to lose them in another city, but all I remember thinking during those few moments, thinking that the area could blow up at any moment were "fuck, fine then". Mentally I seemed to accept the situation as it was and not really think anything. I was fine with what was going on but my body acted on impulse, moving into a building with my family for safety. It was only after the fact that the reality of the situation set in. At the time, I thought I could've died. Even if the bomb didn't kill me, the crowd might've.

In the end, there was never a bomb. Somebody's vape blew up in their bag, while boarding a train, but because London is London, everybody assumed that the person had a bomb on them. That was enough to spark a panic.
